articles.body: NEW DELHI: A three-and-a-half-year-old boy was allegedly physically and sexually assaulted at a private playschool in northeast Delhi’s Maujpur. His father said the child had been troubled for several days before falling seriously ill after returning from school on August 18.CCTV footage purportedly shows the boy being tied to a chair, kicked and pulled by his ears.'Swollen eardrums raise alarm'According to the child’s father, Navneet Chaudhary, his son had been troubled for several days before his condition suddenly worsened on August 18.The father told news agency ANI that the child returned home from school that day, began vomiting and complained of dizziness.He was immediately taken to a paediatrician, who noticed that his eyes were swollen and advised the family to consult an ENT specialist.The ENT doctor allegedly found that the boy’s eardrums in both ears were swollen and appeared to be close to rupturing. The doctor described his condition as critical, the father said.The family subsequently approached the school and asked the management whether the child had been assaulted.CCTV shows boy being tied to chair for hoursThe father said the family later accessed CCTV footage from the day the child had fallen ill.According to him, the footage showed the boy being tied to a chair for hours and allegedly subjected to repeated physical abuse, including being beaten, kicked and having his ears pulled.“I hold the management, owners and principal responsible as well,” the father said, questioning whether school authorities had a duty to monitor CCTV footage and ensure the safety of children.He demanded action against everyone responsible, alleging that the school management had played a major role in the incident.Caretaker arrested, DoE orders probe into playschoolPolice have arrested the caretaker named in the case. articles.body: MUMBAI: Auto-rickshaw and taxi rides will cost more across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR) from midnight on Monday, with revised fares coming into effect from September 1. The state transport department on Sunday released the new tariff cards, giving commuters and drivers a reference point until meters are recalibrated.The minimum autorickshaw fare has been increased from Rs 26 to Rs 27 for the first 1.5 km. The subsequent fare has been fixed at Rs 18.22 per km, rounded off to the nearest rupee. For taxis, the minimum fare has risen from Rs 31 to Rs 33 for 1.5 km, while the subsequent fare will be Rs 21.90 per km.The increase will mean that a 10-km auto ride will cost Rs 182, up from Rs 171, while a taxi ride over the same distance will cost Rs 219, compared with Rs 207 earlier.The revised fares will apply across Mumbai, Thane, Navi Mumbai, Mira-Bhayander, Kalyan and the rest of the MMR.Under the new tariff, an auto ride covering 2 km will cost Rs 36, compared with Rs 34 earlier, while a 5-km journey will cost Rs 91 against Rs 86. For taxis, the fare for 2 km will rise to Rs 44 from Rs 41, while a 5-km ride will cost Rs 110, compared with Rs 103 earlier.Passengers travelling in AC black-and-yellow taxis will have to pay 10% more than the basic black-and-yellow taxi fare.A 25% additional fare will continue to apply for journeys between midnight and 5am.The department has also revised shared-ride fares. The minimum shared-auto fare will now be Rs 12, while the minimum shared-taxi fare will be Rs 11, with both increasing by Re 1.Waiting charges will range between Rs 1 and Rs 2 per minute, depending on the distance covered, officials said.The revised tariff cards will remain valid for three months, during which meters will be recalibrated. articles.title: In 2024, a developer paid $4 million for 83 acres outside Yosemite; two years later the US is considering a land swap for a private access road through the park
articles.summary: US News: A Nevada-based developer is seeking a land exchange that could allow a private road to be built through Yosemite National Park, giving access to an 83.
articles.body: A Nevada-based developer is seeking a land exchange that could allow a private road to be built through Yosemite National Park, giving access to an 83-acre property just outside the park. The Trump administration is considering the proposal, according to documents and people familiar with discussions KQED reported.The property is owned through limited-liability companies operated by Kingsbarn Realty Capital. The company bought the undeveloped 83-acre plot for $4 million in 2024. The land, historically known as Hazel Green Ranch, is located outside Yosemite’s western boundary, about five miles from one of the park’s giant sequoia groves.Kingsbarn CEO Jeff Pori wants to build a short road linking the property to a road inside Yosemite. The proposed route would cross a roughly quarter-mile strip of National Park Service land. In exchange, the Park Service would receive land of equal value elsewhere in California, according to the proposal.The plan has brought back a dispute that has continued for more than two decades. A previous owner of the property had also sought permission to build a private road through Yosemite. That request was rejected by the Park Service, and a court later ruled against the owner.Developer says road would provide direct accessThe property already has an access road, but it is more than 10 miles from a Yosemite entrance. Reaching Yosemite Valley from the property using the existing route would require a circuitous drive of about an hour and a half.The proposed road would provide a much shorter connection to one of Yosemite’s main roads. The property could potentially be developed as a hotel, resort or private residence.The National Park Service is examining whether a land exchange can be carried out under federal law. The Park Service would first need to assess the value of the Yosemite land and identify another property in California of equivalent value.Land exchanges involving federal property are common, but the situation here is unusual because the Park Service would be giving up land within a national park to help provide private access, according to a former Park Service official cited by NOTUS.The value of the Yosemite land is currently being assessed. Sources told NOTUS that the appraisal is difficult because putting a value on a piece of Yosemite is not straightforward, particularly when the proposed access could significantly increase the value of the private property.Similar request was rejected in courtThe current proposal has its roots in an earlier attempt by California developer Lewis Geyser, who previously owned Hazel Green Ranch. Geyser wanted to develop the property as a resort and spent years seeking permission for a private road through Yosemite.The Park Service considered working with Geyser in the early 2000s as part of a broader effort related to development pressure in Yosemite Valley. That plan did not move forward, and the Park Service later refused to allow the proposed private access.Geyser sued the federal government in 2007, seeking to force the issue. He lost in district court and again on appeal in 2012. The courts ruled that he did not have a legal claim to a private road through Yosemite.Although the federal government has an obligation to provide an exit for private property completely surrounded by federal land, the courts found that it did not have to provide a new road when an existing route was available.When Kingsbarn bought the property in 2024, the company approached the Interior Department about reopening the issue.Former Yosemite Superintendent Cicely Muldoon said the request had previously been considered closed. “Whoever bought the land hadn’t done their due diligence and realized that this was not a possibility by law,” she told NOTUS.Former Yosemite Superintendent Don Neubacher also criticised the proposal. He said his office had conducted a legal review of the same land exchange in 2012 and concluded that the Park Service did not have the authority to provide the easement.“There was no legal right for this developer to have access into the Yosemite National Park,” Neubacher told KQED. “The only thing that’s changed is you have a new administration that just seems to be pro-development.”Interior Department denies political pressureIn a statement to KQED, the department said the report relied on anonymous allegations and denied that there had been political pressure to reach a predetermined result. It also rejected claims that the department was secretly working to hand over Park Service land to a private developer.The department said any land exchange or access proposal involving National Park Service land would have to follow federal laws and regulations. That would include environmental review and public notification requirements.Lanny Davis, an attorney working for Kingsbarn, later confirmed that the company was pursuing a land exchange with the Park Service. He argued that the road would provide access to residents of the privately owned property and said it would not endanger endangered species. “It’s simply a road,” Davis said.The proposal has also drawn criticism from conservation groups and Yosemite employees. The National Parks Conservation Association said it strongly opposes the plan and called it a threat to public ownership of Yosemite.The Yosemite National Park employees union also criticised the proposal, saying that giving public land to private interests goes against the role of National Park Service employees.Proposal faces opposition from lawmakersThe proposal was brought to the attention of Congress earlier this year. However, lawmakers overseeing the Land and Water Conservation Fund did not include the Yosemite project on a list of projects they supported for funding.California senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff have also opposed the proposed exchange. Padilla said the Land and Water Conservation Fund exists to protect natural areas, water resources and cultural heritage, and to provide recreation opportunities for Americans. He said projects should be selected on their merits rather than based on connections to senior administration officials.Schiff said Yosemite must be protected from further development and pointed out that courts had already rejected the earlier road proposal.The National Parks Conservation Association’s Neal Desai told KQED that the organisation had verified communications between the administration and Congress about the proposal. “Our national parks right now are in crisis, and Yosemite National Park is in chaos,” Desai said.Jesse Chakrin, director of Fund for People in Parks, also expressed concern about the specific area involved. He described it as a well-loved part of the park known for its dogwood, spring and autumn scenery.The Interior Department has not made a final decision. If the proposal moves ahead, it would still have to undergo the required legal and environmental processes. Conservation groups are also expected to challenge the exchange in court if it is approved.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Bay Area Nepalese community rallies to support flood disaster victims as thousands still missing
articles.summary: "We're trying to hold up each other and show support and sympathy," The Bay Area's Nepalese community is coming together this weekend to support victims of a...
articles.body:
The Bay Area's Nepalese community is coming together this weekend to support victims of a devastating flood and landslide disaster in Nepal that has left families searching for loved ones and communities struggling to recover.

For Berkeley restaurant owner Binita Poudel, the tragedy is deeply personal. Poudel, who owns Taste of the Himalayas on Shattuck Avenue, fears up to 10 relatives may be missing following the deadly flash flood that destroyed parts of a border region in Nepal.

"I called them. Nobody picks up the phone," Poudel said as she described the agonizing wait for information.

Like many Nepalese Americans, Poudel has spent the past several days watching heartbreaking images from her homeland while desperately trying to contact family members. Among those unaccounted for are her husband's uncle and cousin. Despite the uncertainty, she remains hopeful.

"Sometimes, a dream comes true," Poudel said. "We hope they are missing somewhere, and they're going to come out."

To help those affected, Taste of the Himalayas hosted a vigil and fundraiser Sunday night.

The event was meant to bring community members together to pray for the missing while raising money for humanitarian relief efforts.

"A little bit helps. One dollar helps," Poudel said. "It's good for everyone."

The disaster has also shaken Hercules City Councilmember Dilli Bhattari, a Nepal native who spent nearly two days unable to contact his nephew, Prakash, who was traveling in Nepal on a spiritual journey.

"Almost 24 to 48 hours we were disconnected," Bhattari said. "Devastating moments for my family."

Bhattari later learned his nephew was safe after finally making contact. Still, he says many families remain in limbo as they wait for word from relatives in the disaster zone.

"This is one thing I never imagined," Bhattari said. "So fast, so quick, so unimaginable, impacting so many lives."

In response, the City of Hercules hosted its own community vigil to support those affected and provide comfort to local families with ties to Nepal.

"We're trying to hold up each other and show support and sympathy," Bhattari said.

Organizers say both events are intended to support grieving families and raise funds for relief efforts in Nepal.

articles.title: US mayor Joe Anderson dies mysteriously at 45 after sudden collapse on Colorado hike
articles.summary: US News: Joe Anderson lost consciousness and was not breathing while hiking on the lower slopes of Quandary Peak in Summit County, according to local authoriti.
articles.body: Joe Anderson lost consciousness and was not breathing while hiking on the lower slopes of Quandary Peak in Summit County, according to local authorities. Sheriff's deputies were called at about 6.40am after other hikers had already begun CPR.Deputies and medical personnel continued attempts to revive him, but Anderson died at the scene. The cause of death has not been announced and is expected to be determined by the coroner, the Daily Mail reported, citing local authorities. The City of Englewood confirmed his death later Friday.From homelessness work to Englewood councilAnderson entered the Englewood City Council in November 2019 as the representative for District 3 and won another four-year term in November 2023. His council colleagues elected him mayor pro tem in December that year, and his term was scheduled to expire in November 2027.He served in pastoral roles at local churches and helped found Change the Trend, a coalition working on homelessness. The city said his work with the coalition preceded the creation of the Tri-Cities Homelessness Policy Committee, which coordinates policy across Englewood, Littleton and Sheridan.He also spent years coordinating Be a Tool, later renamed the Neighborhood Rehab Project, which organised home repairs for seniors and people with disabilities. He later represented Englewood on the Tri-Cities committee, which worked on regional homelessness services including a navigation centre and a Bridge House employment programme.Anderson was also involved in Englewood's CodeNext overhaul of development rules, backing measures that made it easier to build smaller homes as part of efforts to improve housing affordability.Anderson pushed stormwater overhaul after deadly floodsAfter deadly flooding hit Englewood in 2018, Anderson pressed the city to plan beyond immediate repairs. His position was that Englewood needed a long-term upgrade of its stormwater system without imposing costs that households and businesses could not absorb.The city later completed the $23 million South Englewood Flood Reduction Project, which added detention ponds and upgraded stormwater pipes.‘Always there to lend a hand’: City leaders remember AndersonMayor Othoniel Sierra described Anderson as someone who was “always there to lend a hand” as a friend, neighbour, pastor and elected official. “This is a tremendous loss for our city and our heart goes out to his family and friends during this time of loss,” he said.Outgoing City Manager Shawn Lewis called Anderson “one of the most effective, productive and positive council members I've ever worked with,” and recalled that Anderson had offered to pray for him when his parents were hospitalised during the Covid pandemic.A fundraiser has since been organised for Anderson's wife, Rebecca, and their children. Its organisers described him as a father, husband, friend and neighbour and said memorial details would be announced later.Anderson's District 3 term was due to run until November 2027. Under Englewood's charter, the remaining council members have 30 days to fill the vacancy with a 75% vote. articles.title: Russian strikes destroy 12 million books in Ukraine ahead of new school year
articles.summary: Ukraine says Russia is deliberately attacking its culture, after strikes on publishers and churches.
articles.body:
Viktoria Haidai surveys the mangled remains of the printing press, which should have been busy churning out textbooks ready for the new school year.

The plant, on the edge of Kyiv, was hit during the night by a Russian missile, just as production was ramping up to deliver 1.3 million books – 10% of Ukraine's schoolbooks.

In the ashes there is a charred page from an English language textbook: "My name is William, I'm from the UK. My grandmother lives in Nottingham. It's a beautiful city."

Russia has hit printing presses and publishing houses across Ukraine in a series of recent attacks, destroying 12 million books and damaging other icons of Ukrainian history and culture. Local media report that Russia has destroyed one third of all the books printed in Ukraine this year.

Nothing is salvageable at this Kyiv printing press. Even the pages that survived the flames have succumbed to water damage, from firefighting or exposure to the elements from the collapsed roof.

"I believe it is deliberate on the part of the Russian Federation," says Haidai, commercial director of the Konvi publishing firm. "Over the past two months, some of the largest publishing houses have lost their logistics warehouses, where very large quantities of books were stored.

"The Russians are also destroying printing houses in an attempt to erase Ukraine as a nation. But frankly they will not succeed."

More than 35 publishing facilities have been hit over recent weeks.

But it's not just fresh pages coming under attack. Kyiv's Pochaina second-hand book market was also struck, wiping out hundreds of individual stalls and countless treasured tomes.

Before firefighters had finished extinguishing the blaze, I found Liliya Velyka, a 28-year-old book blogger, raking through the smouldering ruins, seeing if anything could be saved. She clutched a soaking copy of a sci-fi novel.

"Books are saving us and losing this is like losing our hearts," she says.

Museums, art galleries, film studios, libraries, and opera houses have also been damaged. At Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, the capital's large medieval monastery and cultural heritage site, the golden domes of the Dormition Cathedral were hit.

Religious artefacts were moved to safety but a large section of the roof was set ablaze after a drone attack. Repairs are predicted to cost $11.2 million (£8.2m) and will take two years.

The site is also home to Ukraine's museum of books and printing. Unesco listed the complex in 1990, and added it to its register of world heritage sites in danger in September 2023.

At recent celebrations marking 975 years since the monastery's founding, Unesco's Director-General Khaled El-Enany said he was "deeply saddened" to see "the significant damage".

"Unesco firmly condemns all attacks against cultural property protected under international law," he told gathered dignitaries, including President Volodymyr Zelensky.

El-Enany toured the cathedral with Ukraine's minister of culture, Tetyana Berezhna, who told me the cultural and military impacts of Russia's war should not be separated.

"This is an existential war, so Russia wants to destroy us as a nation, to erase us as a nation, like Ukrainians do not exist and have never existed. That's why Russia targets our cultural heritage, the symbols of our presence here for a long time.

"They understand that it's very important for us because we protect our identity, we protect our culture, and Russia wants to ruin everything that it cannot appropriate."

Berezhna says Russia has attacked over 1,900 pieces of Ukrainian heritage and more than 2,000 cultural institutions. Digitisation is part of the strategy to protect art and literature and ensure children can still learn, despite the attacks on physical books.

There are warnings Ukraine's entire publishing sector is under threat and needs international support to remain viable.

At the bombed Kyiv printing press Viktoria Haidai told me protecting the industry was vital to preserving Ukrainian literature. "The word is everything. It is our development, our culture, and our historical heritage that is passed down from generation to generation."

In a 2021 essay, titled On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians, Russian President Vladimir Putin stated that Ukrainians and Russians were one people, and questioned the legitimacy of an independent Ukrainian state and culture.

In a statement to the BBC, the Russian embassy to the UK blamed Ukraine's own government for damage to its cultural heritage, saying monuments had been dismantled and streets renamed. It also claimed cultural sites had been used to conceal military facilities.

The Kremlin has repeatedly denied deliberately hitting civilian targets throughout the five years of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, despite repeated and widespread missile and drone attacks on residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure.

articles.title: The West's sculptures, from the stunning to the slightly odd
articles.summary: From the M5 Willow Man to Cary Grant, the area is home to a variety of figures.
articles.body:
The south west is well known for its artistic culture - Bristol is the home of street art and Glastonbury hosts one of the biggest music festivals.

This might be one of the reasons why you can find so many interesting sculptures in the area: from the huge Willow Man, now sadly falling into disrepair, on the M5, to the Malmesbury monk and more recent creations in Bristol.

Here is our list of where to find these varied and fascinating sculptures.

Bristol, home of Banksy, is the birthplace of street art. This is where you will find some of the best-known sculptures in the West.

Of course, the city is not just home to Banksy but also to Hollywood hero Cary Grant. And where better to start than with a statue in the actor's honour on Millennium Square.

Nearby, there is also a sculpture of a beetle outside Bristol Aquarium by artist Nicola Hicks, based on the rhinoceros beetle, one of various scarab beetles that have one or more horns on their heads.

Bear With Me was installed on Jacob's Wells Road in Bristol in 2020 to mark World Suicide Prevention Day on 10 September.

"I installed this statue during the pandemic, but now people are struggling for different reasons, but just as much. I'm not overly optimistic about things getting better, which is all the more reason why you've got to keep talking about it," the anonymous artist said.

Anyone who has been to the centre of Bristol will have noticed the statue of Neptune. He was cast in lead by the Bristol founder Jon Rendall in 1723. There is also Pero's Bridge, which is currently closed due to a malfunction , which was designed by Eillis O'Connell and named after a slave who lived and died in 18th Century Bristol.

Gloucestershire is iconic for many reasons, but internationally probably most famous for the cheese-rolling competition at Cooper's Hill each May.

There's a gargoyle celebrating the famous race on top of Gloucester Cathedral.

A sculpture honouring a gorilla who lived in a Cotswolds village was erected in Uley.

The gorilla, called John Daniel, was adopted by Alyce Cunningham in 1918, after her brother bought it for £300 in London.

There's also the Forest of Dean sculpture trail, which includes stairs that lead to nowhere that went viral online for baffling passers-by. It also includes a huge pine cone.

The Roman Baths in Bath are an iconic part of the city's history, drawing thousands of visitors every year. The main pool is overlooked by some very eye-catching sculptures.

There are also sculptures just around the corner to the baths, showing angels running along a small ladder on the front of Bath Abbey.

Close to the M5 near Bridgwater, you can find the iconic "Willow Man", which has recently fallen into disrepair .

In Watchet, a beloved goose was memorialised with a sculpture. Derek, the goose, had become a regular sight at Watchet Harbour after migrating to the area more than 10 years ago.

In Wiltshire, there are a few unusual sculptures, including a monk depicted in meditation. It was made by William Lazard. It commemorates the role of monks in Malmesbury's history.

The King Alfred the Great sculpture is a famous landmark in the village of Pewsey and was unveiled in 1913 to commemorate the coronation of George V.

articles.title: First Cambridge outing for all-women fire brigade musical songs
articles.summary: The musical features five pioneering 19th Century women scientists who studied at Cambridge.
articles.body:
Songs from a musical which celebrates a 19th Century physics student will be heard in the city where she studied for the first time.

The musical tells the story of how Hertha Ayrton founded an all-women fire brigade in 1879 at Girton College , then a women's college at Cambridge University.

Music from The Cambridge First All-Ladies Fire Brigade musical will be heard at an Open Cambridge event at the university's Whipple Museum in September.

Co-creator and lyricist Helen Arney said: "We've been working on doing something in Cambridge for so, so long and to finally get there is so lovely."

Alison Giles, the museum's learning coordinator, said bringing music into the museum was "definitely not something we'd usually do".

"But we like to collaborate with others who bring along something that isn't our usual skill set and it's a delight to work with other people who research women scientists," she added.

Whipple Museum of the History of Science takes its name from Robert Stewart Whipple (1871-1953), who gave his collection of 1,000 scientific instruments to the university in 1944, along with a similar number of rare books.

This year's Open Cambridge event is marking the 120th anniversary of Ayrton being awarded the Royal Society's prestigious Hughes Medal - the first and only woman in the entire 20th Century to receive the honour.

Giles said: "We're calling the event Making Marks, because Hertha Ayrton was born Phoebe Marks.

"Dr Patricia Farra, a leading expert on Ayrton, will talk about her specifically and flesh out that story, alongside interactive family talks and hands-on activities."

While the museum does not have any of her instruments - "anything to do with arc lighting is mostly lethally dangerous" - it does have a fume cabinet that once belonged to Ida Freund, another eminent scientist featured in the musical, Giles added.

Arney said: "Freund was an orphan with one leg, dumped at Girton by her guardian, who fell in love with Girton and teaching and taught chemistry at Newnham [another women-only Cambridge college] for decades after.

"Her fume cabinet sucked poisonous air out of the atmosphere during experiments - and our songs will be performed nearby, which is just lovely."

During the event, singer-songwriter Noa Shakhar will perform the Ayrton role, accompanied by Girton graduate and organ scholar Felix Elliot, who is now a musical director in theatre and musicals.

The other pioneering Girton science students featured in the musical are astronomer Annie Russell Maunder , botanist Ethel Sargant and mathematician Charlotte Scott .

Making Marks will take place during Open Cambridge on 12 September . It is supported by University of Cambridge Museums Arts Council England Fund.

articles.summary: The Scottish soap opera, based in the fictional Glasgow district of Shieldinch, is coming to an end after 24 years.
articles.body:
Johnny McKnight has written for River City for almost a decade so, when it was announced that the show was drawing to a close after 24 years, he asked if he could write the final episode.

"Those moments don't come up very often with long-running shows so I thought it might be cathartic and a nice way to say goodbye as a writer," he says.

Details of the episode, which will air on Monday, are a closely-guarded secret but images released showing a bloodied Lenny Murdoch amidst a dramatic fire scene suggest the show's arch-villain, played by Frank Gallagher, is at the centre of it.

He said he felt a huge responsibility to the show's fans to give them a satisfying ending.

He points to cult TV shows whose endings have divided fans - like The Sopranos, Dexter, Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Angel.

Gallagher says: "I'm just part of a massive collective team effort and I hope we've done the fans proud to the end."

He thinks the show has always managed to walk a fine line between comedy and drama.

"River City is what I think it is to be Scottish. Our punches have punchlines.

"We take our trauma and we find a way to tell it in a pub that makes it palatable, and the humour co-exists alongside the drama."

Grant Stott, who played Sam Spiller, says it was the comedy which attracted him to the role.

A broadcaster and pantomime regular, he had limited experience of TV drama.

"There is no way I would have got that kind of experience on another show and for that I will be forever grateful; that was always a bit of a dream for me and so to finally achieve that at this stage of my career was very special.

"If I never get a chance to work in the TV drama industry ever again, I'm all right with that because I've achieved what I wanted to do."

Jenny Hulse, who has played Lenny Murdoch's daughter Amber, has a central role in the finale.

Although it was filmed in April, she says the cast and crew are normally returning to set at this time of year.

"I still think in my muscle memory I'm gearing up for filming again and just waiting for the scripts," she says.

The show, filmed on a now-demolished set in Dumbarton, was famous for its intensive production schedule.

"We were sometimes doing 17 pages a day of quite fast-paced dialogue, whereas if you were on another TV drama set it would be four pages," she says.

"It's like a moving train and when you join you just have to kind of jump on and cling on."

Over 24 years, River City also became known as a hugely important training ground, not just for actors and writers but directors, camera operators, electricians, make-up artists, wardrobe staff and every aspect of the TV industry.

Many have graduated onto other jobs in the industry.

"That legacy and pride in what we did is really special," says Jenny.

"I feel so lucky to have had the opportunity to play the same character and have regular work for 10 years, which is unusual."

Jenny recalled that when she first started out she had only done stage work and some TV.

"Ryan Graham, who directed the finale, started off as a camera trainee way back.

"Holly Jack, who plays Nicole, now directs episodes, as does Sally Reid.

"Cast members become writers, camera operators and directors, and it's incredible to watch that whole conveyor belt of talent.

"It's been a factory. A factory of creativity."

For cast and crew, it's now time to sit back and watch their final piece of work.

As well as the final hour-long episode, there's a one-off documentary, River City: The Last Decade.

For many of fans, it's hard to accept it's over.

"We did an event at the Tron Theatre in Glasgow a couple of weeks ago," says Johnny McKnight.

"We had some of the cast of River City and I was hosting it, and it was just beautiful to see so many fans there.

"They kept asking: 'Will it come back? Do you think it'll have another life?'

"And you feel terrible saying, 'Well, the set has been demolished, so it's looking less likely'."

articles.title: 'Country Babur came from': Owaisi takes dig at PM Modi's Uzbek honour
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi took a dig at the BJP after Prime Minister Narendra Modi was conferred Uzbekistan's highest state honour.PM Mo.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi took a dig at the BJP after Prime Minister Narendra Modi was conferred Uzbekistan's highest state honour.PM Modi was presented with the Order of "Oliy Darajali Dustlik" by Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev during his two-day state visit to the Central Asian country. The honour is Uzbekistan's highest state award.Reacting to the recognition, Owaisi pointed to Uzbekistan's historical connection with Babur, who he said was born in the Fergana Valley in present-day Uzbekistan and founded the Mughal Empire in India."I congratulate the BJP; the very country from which Babur came to India has conferred an award upon the Prime Minister. The Fergana Valley is in Uzbekistan. Wherever the Prime Minister goes these days, he returns with an award. Congratulations. You used to hurl so many insults in Babur's name, yet the people of that very country are now honoring you with an award. The Sangh needs to reflect on this... We hope that members of the Sangh Parivar and RSS supporters will no longer speak of Babur in that manner," he said.The remarks come against the backdrop of the BJP and RSS's frequent criticism of the Mughal period and references to Babur in political discourse, particularly in discussions around the construction of the Ram temple in Ayodhya and India's history.PM Modi, meanwhile, thanked Mirziyoyev for the honour and described him as his "brother". He said India and Uzbekistan would work together for the welfare of the Global South and humanity."My friend, the father of the economic revolution in Uzbekistan, who has served as a role model across this entire region in scaling new heights of development--this two-day visit of mine will always be remembered," PM Modi said.Owaisi's comments on the award came while he was also criticising RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat over his recent remarks on Hindu-Muslim unity. Bhagwat, speaking at the 'One World One Humanity' event in New York, said there was no difference between human beings and that different religious paths led to the same goal.Owaisi described Bhagwat's remarks as an "old trick from the RSS playbook"."What the current RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat has said is an old trick from the RSS playbook. They will never disavow or retract the things the RSS has consistently stated," he said."There is a distinct difference between the speeches they deliver for the outside world and those meant for their own members--this has always been their playbook style," Owaisi said.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
